text: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah): Mr Speaker, before I beg to move that Parliament do adjourn, I would like to thank all the hawkers who came today and for staying with us through this very long debate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Therefore, I appreciate all Members who are choosing to stay, so there is not just a soliloquy between the Minister of State Alvin Tan and myself.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I cannot promise that a speech on "The Road to Decarbonising Our Corporations" will necessarily be all that riveting, but I will do my very best.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As a net energy importer, these are undeniably ambitious targets.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Still, ensuring that our planet is livable in the future, requires that we be bold in setting goals that are adhered to not only by our Government, but also our households and businesses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Today, therefore, I wish to speak about our road toward decarbonisation, with an eye specifically for our nation's corporations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will speak about three related issues: first, I will touch on why focusing on the carbon emissions of the big players alone is not quite good enough; second, I will discuss who we need to train to ensure that our carbon transition efforts eventually succeed; and third, I will explain what role finance can play in all this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I shall close with thoughts on why climate mitigation efforts need not, in fact, undermine our business competitiveness.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The current slate of policies aimed at decarbonisation is comprehensive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In theory, this involves two major steps: decarbonising energy production and electrifying industry, transport and construction.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In practice, this encompasses a diverse mix of policies: carbon taxes, energy efficiency standards and grants, shifting our transportation infrastructure toward electrification and sourcing electricity from alternative sources, both in terms of energy type as well as geographically.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While the Government has, appropriately, taken the lead in these, we will only succeed when businesses are also aligned with the programme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And this requires widespread buy-in by companies that, understandably, face a bottom line and are primarily responsive to their shareholders, who may or may not share the C-suite's enthusiasm for incorporating environmental goals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Ensuring that pro-environment sentiment is widely shared by companies and their shareholders is, therefore, crucial for success.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While this remains below the preferred range for the Workers' Party, not least because it remains somewhat below the median in other advanced economies as well as the costs of carbon capture, we acquiesce to this increase, given how it is, nevertheless, superior to the original status quo.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We have also spoken about how the tax could be adapted according to the contemporaneous state of the economy, to allow firms some latitude to adapt to prevailing macroeconomic conditions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I had, moreover, previously explained why I believe a broad-based carbon tax is not only consistent with public finance principles, but also ensures psychological buy-in from all carbon generators.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I wish to return to this theme here, in the context of businesses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While we may argue that this would largely absolve us from worrying too much about how the remaining companies contribute to emissions, I believe that this mindset is mistaken.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is also because climate change is a global problem and if corporations, including those that are not the primary source emitters, fail to seriously consider their total carbon footprint, they may inadvertently outsource their midstream or downstream activities to other emitters without well-defined carbon action plans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Inattention to midstream activities, such as electricity usage, raw material and equipment procurement and commuting and travel policies, could undermine the upstream efforts by their home country governments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, downstream choices by firms, decisions over their distribution network or how they deal with the end-of-life treatment of their products, all contribute toward the ultimate impact that corporations impose on the climate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is becoming increasingly observed, recognised by observers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is no longer sufficient to pay attention to only so-called Scope 1 emissions, which are the sources an organization owns or controls directly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Scope 2 emissions, which are caused indirectly by a company based on where it chooses to buy its energy and how it uses it, also matter; as does Scope 3 emissions, which are those not covered by Scope 1 or 2, but are nevertheless created by a business' value chain.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This includes more than nine out of 10 Fortune 500 companies and these standards have been road-tested by diverse firms across the world, such as 3M, Acer, Airbus, Coca Cola, Mitsubishi, Pfizer and Shanghai Zidan.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This will include their Scope 1 and 2 emissions, but only listed companies will be required to do so for Scope 3 emissions from 2026.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Larger, non-listed firms are not expected to do so before 2029, which strikes me as an excessive amount of leeway.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Shortening this timeline by a year, for instance, would ensure that they are held to the same standards and expectations as the locally-listed firms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Doing so will also prevent Singapore from losing its competitive edge and status as a global exemplar of climate leadership.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: On its part, the public sector has, appropriately, stepped up.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To complement this report, Statutory Boards will also publish annual environmental sustainability disclosures, starting this fiscal year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such disclosures will offer an important demonstration effect, showing not only what the Government is doing to advance environmental sustainability, but also what is achievable by the private sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Ultimately, a mandatory monitoring and reporting regime will require clear and uniform environmental, social and governance (ESG) standards.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This, in turn, also calls for a whole new set of "green skills": the ability to perform corporate carbon accounting, manage firm assets with an eye toward sustainability and provide reporting on a company's ESG impact.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such capabilities are key to Singapore's long-term survival and adaptability in a carbon-constrained world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But they are also presently scarce, a fact that has been repeatedly highlighted as important needs in the multiple editions of the Skills Demand for the Future Economy report.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A Green Skills Committee was set up in 2023, under the auspices of the Ministry of Trade and Industry.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The group, comprising representatives from Government, unions, industry and academia, placed their focus on two areas: clean energy and sustainability reporting.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If we take this signal seriously, there will be a need to further ramp up training for companies, so that they will be equipped to deliver their climate and sustainability reports at international standards.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, there has to be a body of professional assurance providers that are prepared to audit these emissions reports.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Institutes of Higher Learning will be crucial to help fill this gap.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A quick search on the MySkillsFuture website lists 134 courses related to sustainability reporting, with the most affordable course starting at just $84 for eligible Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If this sounds like a marketing pitch, it is probably a good time for me to declare that I am, in fact, employed at the business school which offers such sustainability-related education.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Still, impending compliance requirements will steadily accelerate the demand for skills in sustainable finance, carbon management, decarbonisation and sustainability risk assessment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These capabilities must be seen as central to Singapore's long-term survival and adaptability in a carbon-constrained world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Businesses need to be able to hire professionals with such tools and skills; and afforded time to train and groom their existing workforce in acquiring green skills and competencies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Although the Government's own Environmental Services Industry Transformation Map is more modest, pointing to around 1,600 professional, manager, executive and technician (PMET) jobs, the ones that are most likely to be filled by locals by this time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To further support upskilling and reskilling in the sector, the Government can offer tax deductions or subsidies for employers with a clear training roadmap, in partnership with accredited or approved training providers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, training providers must also be kept accountable, with education materials subject to checks for accuracy and subject to update and improvement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such consistent review should be required to secure SSG-accreditation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Economic Development Board (EDB) and Enterprise Singapore currently provides funding support for large companies to cover their first sustainability report, which have to be consistent with ISSB's standards.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But with over 600 listed companies in Singapore, all of whom will be required to make climate-related disclosures, they will have their work cut out for them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: More can also be done, however, for our small and medium enterprises (SMEs).

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, it remains unclear what the take-up rate for the proposed target of 200 CCP-S professionals is and how many of these will be operating out of SMEs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And unlike multinationals with substantial budgets that they can dedicate to fulfilling such objectives as well as public reputations and reporting requirements to do so, SMEs are often forced to be selective about the aspects of sustainability that they wish to invest time and resources into.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Direction on what such firms would focus on will undoubtedly be appreciated and the Government can work on a set of guidelines for priority targets.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: SMEs will also need to be able to plan for shifting regulations and community expectations, especially when they venture abroad.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Smaller firms do not have the same capacity to tailor their market research to not only the traditional needs of consumers as well as cost constraints, but also environmental and regulatory considerations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, Enterprise Singapore will need to expand the scope to also provide advisory and assistance on how SMEs can best embed sustainability into their overseas ventures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Just like how we cannot succeed in our climate-mitigation efforts by focusing only on large firms, we, likewise, cannot expect to get to net zero by relying only on public sources of green financing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, our public expenditure needs are vast and the investment gap that has to be met by companies adapting to higher carbon prices, even larger.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is where ESG financing comes into the picture.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is already a burgeoning sustainable finance ecosystem in Singapore, with lending by both private sector financial institutions as well as public sector entities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Still, we should not allow the usual hype over ESG financing to eclipse some of the very real challenges on the ground.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Some financiers have suggested that there is still insufficient, reliable data on green projects to assure them that corporate actions do not merely account to greenwashing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This reprises the concern that I raised earlier, about the need for high-quality standards for reporting and professionals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In the medium run, it may be worthwhile exploring whether subsidies for the green transition should always be directly channeled to businesses or whether there is room to do so via responsible financial intermediaries, who will be in a position to scrutinise business activities and ensure that they truly adhere to green best practices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Some have argued that sustainable projects must entail a "green premium", such that borrowing costs would be higher than the market rate for comparable brown opportunities, with the shift toward ESG-conscious investing, implying that pollutive enterprises now frequently face higher costs of capital, as perhaps they should, if we expect to wean ourselves off such dirty technologies in the longer run.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet the evidence remains amply unclear as to whether responsible investing must necessarily imply inferior returns.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Allow me to close by addressing one of the most common, knee-jerk fears to the pursuit of climate objectives especially held by businesses: that it will raise costs and, hence, undermine competitiveness.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This claim, while seemingly intuitive, is, at best, incomplete.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While the explanations for why going green may not only be environmentally but also financially sustainable are both complex and multifaceted, the logic can be expressed in a more straightforward manner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Think about any kind of investment: whether it be in knowledge or the latest technology or even old-school buildings and equipment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These investments always take time before they pay off.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Businesses do not set aside earnings for research and development, artificial intelligence or capital expenditure for fun.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: They do it because they expect, years, perhaps, even decades down the road, they will be in a more profitable position with these investments, than without.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The same can be said for spending on sustainability and green technology.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While it may sometimes seem like the money goes directly into a cost black hole, in reality, these are truly investments, which will pay off more in the future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For example, over the past decade, solar and wind power have become cost-competitive with fossil fuels, even without any financial support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, if irreversible climate change were to become entrenched, business costs will, themselves, be elevated by higher insurance and other business costs due to natural disasters, as we have observed in countries as diverse as Bangladesh, Mexico, Poland, Spain and Thailand.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In the meantime, any old brown job that is being displaced means new jobs will also, inevitably, be created.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While there is no sugarcoating how companies will have to dig into their pockets, at least in the near term, to decarbonise, in the future, they will reap the benefits of their green investments, which will not only be better for their own bottom lines, but also for the only planet that we all inhabit, too.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So long as we, as a society and economy, continue to direct technological change in favour of clean, rather than dirty inputs, we will also be able to ultimately realise the dream of sustainable growth for our companies and communities, of course, our children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This balance is key in every single decision we make to move Singapore towards a low-carbon future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: To meet our commitment, we must take, as the Member said, bold steps.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: But we must also pace ourselves carefully, consider global and technological developments and, of course, the impact to our companies and to our people.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We have made decisive moves at the national level.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Please allow me to touch on some of these moves.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: First, the carbon tax, which the Member raised.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The carbon tax is a primary lever in our decarbonisation toolkit.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: It sends an economy-wide signal to our companies to decarbonise.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: That said, we must be mindful and careful about the carbon tax rate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: In fact, we were the first in our region to implement such a carbon price.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This coverage is one of the most comprehensive already in the world and it rises to 90%, if you account for excise duties on transport fuels.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We are also striking a delicate balance between covering this final 10% of emissions and the added administrative burden, including of reporting and verification.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We need to balance between that as well as the burden to our companies and to our people.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The Member also talked a bit about our energy mix.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Besides setting a price on carbon, we have also intensified our efforts to decarbonise our power grid, which will help all companies address their Scope 2 emissions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: First, we are maximising our use of solar energy, which is the most viable source of renewable energy available to us.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Third, we are exploring nascent low-carbon alternatives, such as hydrogen, geothermal energy and newer, nuclear energies and assessing how they can be applied to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Minister Tan See Leng talked about that earlier this morning.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Fourth, we are also engaging industry players to address demand.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We recognise that companies in this world face both opportunities as well as challenges as we make this transition to net-zero together.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: More large corporates are setting science-based climate targets, including here in Asia.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Well, it generates higher demand for clean energy sustainability solutions and carbon credits for those hard-to-abate emissions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: It also generates new green growth opportunities in areas, such as offshore wind and carbon services and trading.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: At the same time, we also acknowledge that companies face challenges to adopt these low carbon alternatives and operations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: For example, they may need to deploy new technology that is probably more expensive and less proven, and make adjustments to their processes with possible downtime in their production.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Capital providers and clients are also increasingly demanding that companies report and reduce their emissions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Workers, as the Member mentioned, may also need different skills to take on new or transformed roles.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Therefore, we are supporting our companies at different stages of their sustainability journey, to build capabilities, develop their decarbonisation plans, access financing and to train, upskill and reskill our workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We are working with our trade associations and chambers (TACs) and financial institutions in this endeavour.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This is an important first step for a company to understand its baseline emissions and develop a decarbonisation strategy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Here are some ways we are helping; the Member enumerated some ways too.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Companies under Singapore’s phased climate reporting requirements can get started early on their ISSB-aligned reports, by using the Sustainability Reporting Grant introduced by EDB and Enterprise Singapore, a point made by the Member.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: SMEs can also use our SME Sustainability Reporting Programme to prepare their first sustainability reports and this is much more affordably, with the help of appointed service providers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: SMEs can also tap the Singapore Business Federation's Emission Factors Registry and the Monetary Authority of Singapore's (MAS') Gprnt to adopt digital solutions to smoothen their carbon accounting and reporting process.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: In fact, Gprnt can help an SME automatically translate its day-to-day activities and data from local digital platforms, such as Myinfo Business and Corppass, into a basic sustainability report.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: With the company's consent, Gprnt can directly share this report with financing and supply chain partners, which will help these SMEs cut down their reporting time and costs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Beyond that, we are also helping companies as they chart and implement their decarbonisation strategy, working with industry players, such as the Sustainability Alliance, which comprises 18 TACs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: TACs, such as the Singapore Logistics Association, have been working very closely with my colleagues at Enterprise Singapore to develop sectoral sustainability playbooks to guide companies on practical, sector-specific steps to the green transition.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I launched this playbook with SLA in February.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We also have "Queen Bee" companies, which are important.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Companies, such as City Developments Limited and SingPost, are helping their suppliers build capabilities in emissions measurement as well as decarbonisation, to better meet their sustainable procurement criteria.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The Government provides funding to help companies to implement green initiatives, with higher support levels for SMEs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Companies and SMEs can use the Energy Efficiency Grant and, for larger companies, the Resource Efficiency Grant for Emissions to implement energy efficiency projects and enjoy longer-term energy efficiency gains.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This particular grant helped a local company called Mlion Corporation to build an innovative B2B steel marketplace for pre-owned construction steel materials.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: So, by using that, you are already seeing some savings.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: So, the Member's point about green finance is key.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: That is why we are catalysing private green capital to support companies in their transition, leveraging Singapore’s status as a sustainable finance hub.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: In fact, as the Member observed, Singapore is ASEAN’s largest market for green, social, sustainability and sustainability-linked bonds and loans, accounting for over half of the ASEAN market.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Enterprise Singapore also recently launched programmes with DBS and United Overseas Bank to offer preferential financing rates for sustainability action, including decarbonisation and green initiatives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Companies need talent to drive this low-carbon transition.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: That is why we are indeed reskilling and upskilling workers to take on these newly created roles.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The Member mentioned the Green Skills Committee, which we launched last year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: It is developing skills and training programmes in areas such as sustainability reporting and assurance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: SSG is also working with the Institute of Banking and Finance to extend its accredited sustainable finance courses beyond financial institutions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This is to build sustainable finance capabilities among real-economy companies, particularly our SMEs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: So, there is a comprehensive suite of training.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: These are examples of how we are preparing our people for this green transition.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And it is really fitting that we close what is likely our last Parliamentary Sitting of the year on this very important issue.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Because it concerns the future of our island nation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Climate change, Mr Speaker, is an existential threat to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: As an island, we are vulnerable to rising sea levels.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And as a densely populated tropical city, we are vulnerable to severe heat stress.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: On our part, our Government will continue to set clear direction and build an enabling environment for the green transition.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We will chart forward-looking decarbonisation pathways and partner industry to build green capabilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: But beyond government and businesses, we all too, as consumers, must also play an important role in this green transition.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We could choose low or zero-carbon alternatives in our lifestyles, for example.
